1	# Haven MVP Design
2	
3	## What Haven is
4	
5	Haven is a searchable private memory network for the people you know.
6	
7	You save people, you connect with them through one central hub, and later you find any of them by any detail you remember.
8	
9	The phone is the product.
10	You meet people holding your phone, so Haven is phone-first and the feel of the app matters as much as the features.
11	
12	## The MVP in one sentence
13	
14	An iPhone app where you have a profile, you connect with people in one tap, and every person you know becomes searchable by any detail you remember about them.
15	
16	## Stack decisions (and why)
17	
18	### Client: native SwiftUI
19	
20	We build the client natively in SwiftUI rather than wrapping the web app.
21	
22	Haven is a human and social app where the entire value is how it feels to hold, connect, and browse people.
23	Gesture physics, spring transitions, haptics, momentum scroll, and keyboard behavior are the product, not polish added later.
24	A WebView has a ceiling on that feel that native does not, so native is the right tool for what we care most about.
25	
26	Development cost and speed are explicitly not the deciding factor here.
27	Long-term quality and the tactile experience win.
28	
29	### Backend: Convex (kept)
30	
31	We keep Convex as the backend.
32	
33	Going native is a client rebuild, not a full-system rewrite.
34	The Convex data model, functions, and auth logic largely persist.
35	Convex ships a Swift client and Clerk ships an iOS SDK, so the native app talks to the same backend.
36	
37	Those mobile SDKs are newer and less battle-tested than their web counterparts.
38	That is the one real cost of going native, and Phase 0 exists to de-risk it before we build anything real on top.
39	
40	We change one foundation at a time.
41	Going native is already one big change, so we do not also swap the database at the same moment.
42	
43	One caveat that shapes the client design: Convex is online-first and its Swift client has no durable offline write queue.
44	The capture moment happens at events with bad connectivity, so the client owns a small local pending queue (see The offline rule below).
45	
46	### Auth: Clerk with custom UI
47	
48	We use Clerk, with fully custom UI.
49	
50	Clerk supports headless custom flows where we build every screen ourselves in SwiftUI and call Clerk methods underneath.
51	On iOS this is the normal path, so we get full control of the sign-in and sign-up feel while Clerk carries the security machinery.
52	
53	We include Sign in with Apple from day one.
54	App Store guideline 4.8 requires it once any third-party login (for example Google) is offered, and it is also the lowest-friction option for the App Clip later.
55	
56	We do not build our own auth system.
57	The hard parts of auth are invisible and dangerous: password hashing, session token rotation, OAuth, verification, rate limiting, and breach handling.
58	Getting any of those subtly wrong leaks user data, and Haven lives or dies on trust.
59	
60	### Repo layout
61	
62	Monorepo.
63	The iOS app lives in an `ios/` directory next to the existing `convex/` backend and `src/` web app.
64	The web app stays alive as the waitlist and marketing surface, not as a product client.
65	
66	### Datastore note: Convex now, revisit later
67	
68	Haven's long-term data shape is relational plus graph plus vector.
69	Attributes are relational, the connection network is a graph, and semantic memory search is vector.
70	
71	That shape fits a Postgres-family system (for example plain managed Postgres with pgvector, or Polygres) better than a pure document store in the long run.
72	
73	We do not adopt that now.
74	The MVP needs none of graph traversal or hybrid retrieval, Polygres specifically is a very young product to bet a foundation on, and we refuse to stack two risky rewrites at once.
75	When the graph and matching phase becomes real, we evaluate the datastore against actual requirements.
76	Managed Postgres plus pgvector is the safe pick, Polygres is the ambitious one, and the small three-table model keeps migration cheap if we ever move.
77	
78	## Design principles
79	
80	The core loop is Capture, Refine, Recall, Reach.
81	If those feel great, Haven works.
82	If they do not, no feature saves it.
83	
84	In the MVP, each stroke of the loop has a concrete form:
85	Capture is connecting or manually saving a person.
86	Refine is opening a contact and editing its memory notes.
87	Recall is search.
88	Reach is tapping the preferred contact method.
89	The swipe review queue is the future upgrade of Refine, not its definition, so the MVP notes editor is a money screen and not an afterthought textbox.
90	
91	Single-player value comes first.
92	The directory, manual save, and search are useful even if you are the only Haven user in the world, so we build that before the network layer.
93	
94	Reduce friction at the moment of input.
95	Input is the hardest thing to get, so every capture step must be fast enough to not break a live conversation.
96	
97	The offline rule: capture never fails.
98	Events have terrible network, so every capture action writes locally first and syncs when connectivity returns.
99	The UI shows pending state, never an error, at the moment of capture.
100	
101	Feel is validated early, not last.
102	Phase 1 includes a hero-interaction spike built to the full quality bar, so we learn our SwiftUI ceiling in week two instead of after four phases of plumbing.
103	
104	Protect the scope.
105	The vision is large, and every idea will try to pull us off the core, so the roadmap stays parked until the core is proven.
106	
107	## Scope: what is in, what is out
108	
109	In for MVP:
110	
111	Your own profile and shareable card.
112	Connect with another Haven user in one tap (mutual, no request and accept dance, because the act of connecting in person is the consent).
113	Manually save a person who is not on Haven yet, including a photo.
114	A directory of everyone you know.
115	Memory notes on every contact, with a first-class editing experience.
116	Search by structured attribute filters plus keyword matching over notes.
117	A local pending queue so capture works offline.
118	Sign in with Apple alongside other login options.
119	In-app account deletion (required by App Store guideline 5.1.1).
120	
121	Out for MVP, parked but not forgotten:
122	
123	App Clip connect-back for non-users.
124	Semantic natural-language search.
125	The swipe review queue and voice capture (the upgrade of Refine).
126	LinkedIn scraping and enrichment.
127	Calendar smart-matching.
128	Selective card sharing (per-person control of which fields are revealed).
129	Rotating connect tokens (anti-replay).
130	Bluetooth radar and ambient detection.
131	Any social, matching, or feed layer.
132	The future idea of the system reading your messages to suggest people.
133	
134	## Data model (Convex)
135	
136	Three tables. This is the whole backend for MVP.
137	
138	### profiles
139	
140	A Haven user's own card, the canonical source of their data.
141	Fields: name, photo, socials (IG, X, WhatsApp, Telegram, phone, and any other handles), preferred contact method, and structured attributes (city, company, role).
142	
143	### contacts
144	
145	Your directory.
146	Each row is one person you know, and it uses an overlay model.
147	
148	A contact always stores your layer: memory notes, your own custom fields, and a photo you attached.
149	If the person is a connected Haven user, the contact also holds a reference to their live profile, and the app renders the merge of their canonical data plus your layer.
150	If the person is not on Haven, the contact stores their data directly: display name, structured attributes, social handles, preferred contact, photo.
151	
152	Reference, not copy, for connection-backed contacts.
153	Copying at connect time would let contacts go stale, which is the exact problem Haven exists to solve.
154	With the overlay, their card stays current and your memories stay yours.
155	
156	Search runs over this table (merged view for connection-backed rows).
157	
158	### connections
159	
160	Mutual edges between two Haven users.
161	When two users connect, one edge is created and a contact row appears in each person's directory referencing the other's profile.
162	
163	### Deletion semantics
164	
165	When a user deletes their account, their profile and canonical data are removed.
166	Contacts in other people's directories that referenced the deleted profile collapse to a frozen snapshot owned by the directory owner, like a phone contact.
167	Your memory of a person is yours, but the live canonical data belongs to them and leaves with them.
168	
169	The model is deliberately small so it stays portable if we ever leave Convex.
170	
171	## Screens (SwiftUI)
172	
173	Onboarding: Clerk sign-in (Sign in with Apple first), then create your profile (name, photo, socials, preferred contact, city, company, role).
174	
175	My Card: your profile as a card that you show people. Editable.
176	
177	Connect: start or accept a connection, and save a non-user manually.
178	
179	Directory (home): the list of your contacts with search on top. Money screen one.
180	
181	Contact detail with the notes editor: one person's attributes, socials, a tappable preferred-contact that opens straight into WhatsApp or IG or phone, and your memory notes with a first-class editing experience. Money screen two.
182	
183	Add contact manually: for people not on Haven (name, photo, socials, notes).
184	
185	Search: filter chips for structured attributes (company, city, role) plus a keyword field over notes, and results.
186	
187	## The search contract (MVP)
188	
189	Be honest about what MVP search is, so testing measures scope and not a broken promise.
190	
191	MVP search answers: filter by company, city, or role, combined with keywords that appear in your notes.
192	"Company: LinkedIn, city: SF" works.
193	Keyword "Spain shirt" works if those words are in the note.
194	
195	MVP search does not answer natural-language sentences.
196	Typing "who do I know at LinkedIn who lives in SF" into a box is the semantic fast-follow, not v1.
197	Fuzzy matching is limited, so a misspelled name may not match.
198	
199	The search UI is designed as filters plus keywords, so users are never invited to type a sentence that will return nothing.
200	
201	## The connect flow (MVP version)
202	
203	For v1 we support the both-have-Haven path only.
204	
205	Two users connect in person, and both directories update mutually with each other's card.
206	No separate request and accept step, because connecting in person is the consent.
207	
208	If the other person is not on Haven, you save them manually.
209	That manual save is the fallback floor.
210	
211	Known hole, accepted consciously: a screenshot of a connect code works forever for anyone holding the image.
212	Fine at trusted-cohort scale.
213	Rotating tokens are the later fix and live on the roadmap.
214	
215	The App Clip connect-back for non-users is the very next thing after v1.
216	It is not blocking, because the first small cohort can all be on Haven for testing.
217	
218	## Core use cases (start to end)
219	
220	The core loop is Capture, then Refine, then Recall, then Reach, wrapped by onboarding.
221	
222	### A. Set up my card (onboarding, once)
223	
224	I download Haven and sign in.
225	I build my card: photo, name, my handles, and I mark the one I actually want people to reach me on.
226	I add where I live, where I work, and my role.
227	Now I have a card I can show anyone, and I am findable by the people I connect with.
228	
229	### B. Meet someone and capture them (Capture)
230	
231	I am at an event and meet someone.
232	If they have Haven, we connect and their card lands in my directory instantly with all their details, no typing.
233	If they do not, I add them in a few seconds with a name, a handle, and a quick note.
234	Either way they are now in my directory, captured without breaking the conversation, even if the venue Wi-Fi is dead.
235	
236	### C. Add context (Refine)
237	
238	Later that night I open Haven, go to the person I met, and drop a memory into their notes: "met at Katrin, wore a Spain shirt, works on Amazon's research team, we talked soccer."
239	Thirty seconds, and the person is richly remembered instead of a blank name I will forget.
240	
241	The future version of this step is the swipe queue: a stack of today's people, swipe left to skip, swipe right to keep and drop a voice or text memory.
242	The MVP version is the notes editor, which is why the notes editor has to be excellent.
243	
244	### D. Find someone by what I remember (Recall)
245	
246	Weeks later I need that person but I have forgotten their name.
247	I filter by company LinkedIn and city SF, or I search the keyword "Spain shirt."
248	Haven pulls them up.
249	This is the thing other apps cannot do, because they only search by name or a username that might have changed, while Haven searches by everything I know about a person.
250	
251	The natural-language version of this ("who was the guy in the Spain shirt from Katrin") arrives with semantic search as the first fast-follow.
252	
253	### E. Reach out (Reach)
254	
255	I found them, and their card shows the contact method they actually want to be reached on.
256	I tap it and it opens straight into WhatsApp or IG or their number.
257	I never had to remember which platform they prefer or dig through five apps, because Haven centralized it.
258	
259	Everything on the roadmap just makes one of these steps lower-friction or richer.
260	
261	## Build order
262	
263	We sequence so something useful exists as early as possible.
264	The directory, manual save, and search have single-player value, so we build that before the network.
265	
266	### Phase 0, Foundations
267	
268	Apple Developer account, Xcode and SwiftUI project in `ios/`, wire in the Convex Swift client and Clerk iOS SDK.
269	
270	Definition of done, and it is strict: sign in with Clerk on a physical iPhone, call an authenticated Convex query with the Clerk-issued token, and see a live update pushed to the screen.
271	Reading public data does not count.
272	The authenticated seam is the riskiest integration in the whole plan, and Phase 0 exists to prove it end to end.
273	
274	Also in Phase 0: verify App Store name availability for "Haven" (the name is crowded, and a "Haven: ..." subtitle form may be needed).
275	
276	### Phase 1, Profile plus the hero spike
277	
278	Onboarding, create and edit profile, My Card.
279	
280	Plus the hero-interaction spike: one moment (the connect animation, or directory scroll and card open) built to the full quality bar with real springs, haptics, and gesture physics.
281	This validates our SwiftUI ceiling early and sets the standard everything else inherits.
282	
283	### Phase 2, Directory, manual save, contact detail
284	
285	Now you can save and open people, and the app is dogfoodable immediately.
286	The local pending queue ships here, because capture must never fail offline.
287	The notes editor ships here and gets money-screen treatment.
288	Prototype the contacts data model before building this phase (see todo.md, Prototype checkpoints).
289	
290	### Phase 3, Search
291	
292	Filter chips plus keyword search over the directory, per the search contract above.
293	
294	### Phase 4, Connect
295	
296	Connect two Haven users with an auto mutual connection, turning a private notebook into a network.
297	
298	### Phase 5, Polish pass
299	
300	Haptics, transitions, and gesture physics across every screen, extending the hero-spike standard to the whole app.
301	For Haven this is the product, so it gets its own real phase, not leftover time.
302	
303	### Phase 6, Distribution
304	
305	TestFlight to the waitlist cohort first, then App Store submission.
306	Submission needs the compliance checklist below done.
307	
308	## Prototype checkpoints
309	
310	The spots worth a throwaway prototype, and the rule for when, are tracked in todo.md under "Prototype checkpoints".
311	In short: the contacts overlay, connection, and deletion data model is the one high-value prototype, done right before Phase 2; a couple of roadmap items (calendar matching, swipe queue) get one when built.
312	UI and feel questions go through SwiftUI previews in Xcode, not the web prototype skill.
313	
314	## App Store compliance checklist
315	
316	In-app account deletion (guideline 5.1.1), wired to the deletion semantics above.
317	Sign in with Apple offered alongside any third-party login (guideline 4.8).
318	Privacy policy URL and App Privacy nutrition labels.
319	Permission strings for camera (connect scanning) and photo library (contact photos).
320	
321	## Testing strategy
322	
323	Convex functions keep the existing vitest TDD flow: write the failing test, implement, run the suite.
324	The Swift side gets view-model unit tests for logic (search filtering, pending queue, merge rendering of overlay contacts).
325	UI feel is verified by hand on device, because springs and haptics cannot be asserted in a unit test, but everything with logic in it is test-first.
326	
327	## Roadmap (fast-follows and later)
328	
329	In rough order after MVP.
330	
331	Semantic natural-language search, the AI-directory magic, using Convex vector search over memory notes.
332	
333	App Clip connect-back, so a non-user can join the connection in the moment with a single Sign in with Apple tap, without an install wall.
334	
335	The swipe review queue with voice capture, upgrading Refine from the notes editor to a thirty-second nightly ritual.
336	
337	LinkedIn enrichment, where you paste a profile link and Haven scrapes it into structured, searchable data.
338	
339	Calendar smart-matching, where the time you connected with someone plus your calendar pre-fills "met at X" for you to confirm or edit.
340	
341	Selective card sharing, per-person control over which fields a connection reveals, because all-or-nothing sharing will be an early user ask.
342	
343	Rotating connect tokens, closing the screenshot-replay hole.
344	
345	Bluetooth radar as an explicit foreground event mode, and only later a wearable beacon if demand proves out.
346	
347	The social and matching layer, opt-in and machine-only, where shared interests surface abstract matches without exposing the underlying data.
348	
349	The far-future idea of the system reading your messages to suggest people, noted only so we do not lose it.
350	
351	## Concerns
352	
353	These are the unsolved friction problems at the heart of the product.
354	They are mostly behavioral and psychological, not technical, which is what makes them hard.
355	None of them are blockers, but they are the things most likely to decide whether Haven actually works.
356	
357	### 1. Friction to manually add people
358	
359	Manual entry is slow relative to a live conversation.
360	It is framed as the fallback floor, but until the App Clip ships it is the default path at real events, because most strangers will not have Haven.
361	So the piece we treated as an edge case carries most of the early capture load, and if it feels like data entry people will not do it mid-conversation.
362	The open question is how fast and low-effort we can make manual add, and whether there is a lighter in-the-moment gesture than filling a form.
363	
364	### 2. Friction to manually add dynamic context
365	
366	Dynamic context is the memory only a human holds: how you think about someone, why they matter, the detail you would forget.
367	There is probably no machine shortcut here, because no scrape or API can know what is in your head, so this input is inherently manual.
368	That means the lever is not technical, it is psychological: how do we trigger the moment, and how do we make putting it in feel frictionless or even rewarding rather than like a chore.
369	Direction worth exploring: the right timing of the prompt, making the act feel like a small reward, and the lightest possible input (a sentence, a voice note) instead of structured fields.
370	This is an open design problem, not a solved one.
371	
372	### 3. Swipe-to-approve context assumes re-engagement that may not happen
373	
374	The swipe review ritual assumes people open the app later, on the couch, to process the day.
375	Many will not.
376	Deferred review depends on re-engagement that we cannot count on, so the whole "nightly ritual" model may be fragile.
377	The open question is whether context should be captured more in the moment instead of deferred, or whether a well-timed reminder can reliably pull people back, and this is exactly why the swipe queue is a fast-follow to test rather than an MVP assumption.
378	
379	## Open questions and risks
380	
381	The Convex Swift client and Clerk iOS SDK are newer than their web versions.
382	This is the main technical risk, mitigated by Phase 0's strict definition of done.
383	
384	WebView was rejected precisely because of gesture feel, so native quality is now on us to deliver, starting with the Phase 1 hero spike rather than waiting for Phase 5.
385	
386	Real-world validation has a cold-start trap: at actual events, strangers will not have Haven, so most capture falls to manual entry until the App Clip ships.
387	Judge the MVP on single-player value (do testers return to search their directory), not on network effects it cannot have yet.
388	
389	The datastore may need to move to a Postgres-family system when the graph and matching phase arrives, and we accept re-evaluating it then rather than now.
390

1	# Haven iOS (Phase 0 foundations)
2	
3	This is the native SwiftUI client scaffold for Haven.
4	Its only job in Phase 0 is to prove the riskiest seam in the whole native plan: Clerk sign-in on iOS authenticating a real Convex query.
5	
6	See `../mvp-design.md` for the full plan. Phase 0's strict definition of done is: sign in with Clerk on a physical iPhone, call an authenticated Convex query, and see a live result.
7	
8	## Status
9	
10	The scaffold is written against the pinned SDK versions and mirrors the `clerk-convex-swift` package's own example app, so the integration pattern is verified.
11	What a green build proves and does not prove:
12	
13	- A green simulator build proves the code compiles against the real SDKs and the Swift packages resolve and link.
14	- It does NOT prove authentication works, because nothing executes during a build.
15	
16	Finishing the Phase 0 DoD is a human step: add the two config values, create the Clerk JWT template, and run on a device (below).
17	
18	## Prerequisites
19	
20	- Xcode 26.x with an installed iOS simulator runtime (open Xcode once, or run `xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS`).
21	- XcodeGen: `brew install xcodegen`.
22	
23	## Generate and open
24	
25	The `.xcodeproj` is generated from `project.yml` and is git-ignored.
26	
27	```sh
28	cd ios
29	xcodegen generate
30	open Haven.xcodeproj
31	```
32

Read the design doc, todo, the Phase 0 iOS scaffold, and the Convex side. Here's where I land.

## Short answer on inspiration: yes, but the narrow kind

Not mood boards. Static Dribbble/Pinterest shots are close to useless for what Phase 1 is actually de-risking, because feel is motion, gesture, and haptics - none of which survive a screenshot.

What's worth an hour: hold 3-5 apps on your actual phone that nail card presentation and profile editing, and write down specific moments to steal. Which spring, which gesture, what happens on release. That gives the hero spike a concrete target instead of "make it feel good." There's an `apple-design` skill installed that covers exactly this vocabulary (spring physics, interruptible transitions, materials), so I'd run the reference pass through that lens.

Hard timebox it. The doc's own stance is that feel gets iterated in Xcode previews on device, not in mockups. Inspiration sets the target, then we build.

## The ordering I'd push for: hero spike first, CRUD second

The doc lists both in Phase 1 but doesn't say which comes first. I think the spike goes first, and it's not a close call.

The spike is the only thing in Phase 1 that can invalidate the native bet. Its stated job is to tell us our SwiftUI ceiling "in week two instead of after four phases of plumbing." Profile schema and CRUD are low-risk plumbing that we'd potentially throw away if the feel ceiling disappoints. So: build the spike against a hardcoded mock profile (it's pure motion, it needs no backend at all), learn what we learn, then wire real data behind it.

## Two things the plan was undercounting

**Custom sign-in is still Phase 1 work.** Phase 0 shipped with Clerk's prebuilt `AuthView` in place - the iOS README says so explicitly, and the design doc puts custom auth UI in Phase 1, including Sign in with Apple from day one (App Store guideline 4.8 requires it). That's a headless-Clerk SwiftUI build. Easy to forget because Phase 0 "already did auth."

**The profile photo is a real sub-task,** not a checkbox. PHPicker plus a Convex `_storage` upload.

## The backend constraint, now confirmed

Today's `profiles` table is three fields: `userId`, `username`, `updatedAt`. Built for the old Haven Meet handle exchange. The MVP profile needs name, photo, socials, preferred contact, city, company, role.

I checked whether the legacy web app is actually dead, since the design doc calls web "waitlist and marketing only." It isn't dead - `resolveView` in `src/lib.ts:227` still sends any authenticated visitor to the full `home` product, which calls `profiles.getMyProfile`, `setUsername`, `meetExchange`, plus the whole `people`/`captures`/`loveAlarm`/`sharedNotes` surface.

So the schema change is additive: new fields go on as optional, web keeps working, nothing breaks. That's the right call regardless - reshaping a shared table to save a few nullable fields is a bad trade.

Separately, that whole web product surface is now orphaned code. Not a Phase 1 decision, but worth deciding soon whether it gets deleted or formally parked.

## Proposed sequence

1. Inspiration pass, ~1 hour, on-device, motion-specific
2. Hero spike: My Card, mock data, full quality bar
3. Extend `profiles` schema plus mutations (existing vitest TDD flow)
4. Onboarding and profile edit wired to real data, still behind the prebuilt AuthView
5. Photo upload
6. Swap the front door: custom sign-in UI plus Sign in with Apple

Steps 4 and 6 split on purpose. Building the profile half against the existing AuthView means you can dogfood sooner and the custom auth work doesn't block anything.

- `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`: "Prefer quality, simplicity, robustness, scalability, and long-term maintainability over development cost and speed."
- `mvp-design.md`: "Development cost and speed are explicitly not the deciding factor here."

Let me look at what visual language Haven already has, since you built one.

Before I answer the design question - I found something that changes the input.

**The inspiration you're looking for is already in this repo, and you built it.**

`src/sky.ts` is not a decorative star field. Read its own header comment: *"every person's card is a unique patch of space, minted deterministically from their identity. Same person, same sky, forever."*

What's already built and tested there:

- Every person gets their own constellation, derived from who they are. Not random, not assigned - minted from their name. It never changes.
- The constellation is drawn with a minimum spanning tree, with the comment *"which is why real star charts look calm instead of criss-crossed."* Calm was already the goal.
- `buildCluster` shrinks that same figure onto a map so the shape on the atlas is recognizably the shape on their card. The comment says *"identity, not decoration."*
- `atlasLayout` spirals everyone you know around you in a golden-angle field, newest nearest the center.
- `buildDust` is one shared field of faint stars seeded from a fixed string, *"so the whole sky twinkles as one"* - and it's deliberately dim, because *"dust must never compete with a person's stars."*

That is the entire list you gave me. Invisible connection: you and everyone you know are lights in one shared sky. Memory leaving traces: your sky is permanently yours. Emotional quiet: the dust is dim on purpose so people stand out. Softness and mystery: a constellation is a shape you have to look at twice to see.

You already solved this. It's in React and it needs to move to SwiftUI. That's a much better starting point than a mood description, because it's a working system with tests, not a vibe.

## The tension you need to resolve, and my proposed answer

You asked for two things that pull apart if I take them literally.

Notion is flat, plain, monochrome, no glow, functional. *Your Name* is saturated twilight, comet light, floating particles. Blend them naively and you get mud - a form with sparkles on it, which reads as cheap.

Here's the reconciliation I'd build on. Think about what that film actually looks like most of the time. A classroom. A train. A convenience store. Someone cooking dinner. It's ordinary life rendered with extraordinary attention to light. The magic moments - twilight, the comet - are rare and brief. The film earns them by being quiet everywhere else.

So the principle for Haven:

> **Plain content, quiet light. The magic is rare, and the user always causes it.**

Which means:

- Layout, type, and copy stay Notion-plain. Generous space, ordinary words, no ornament. This is the "anyone belongs here" part, and it's most of the app.
- Light is the only expressive material, and it lives *behind* content, never on top of it. Nothing glows just to look nice.
- Magic is earned and rare. The card forming. A connection being made. Not every tap.
- "Memory leaving traces" means light responds only to something the user did. That's the difference between traces and a screensaver.

One consequence worth naming: the existing sky is rich - 150 faint stars, three nebulae, giants, diffraction flares, a shooting star. You now want minimalist. So the port to SwiftUI is a **reduction**, not a copy. Keep the system, dial the density down hard. That's a real decision, not a detail.

## Your onboarding edits, taken

Name required. Photo optional. Location optional. Interests cut from onboarding entirely, editable later in profile. Socials plus preferred contact as the actual core, since that's the thing the whole product pays off on.

One thing you should know before I write it down: `mvp-design.md` has company and role in the profile, and Phase 3 search filters on **company, city, and role**. Your minimalist flow drops company and role. That's fine for onboarding, but they need to exist in the schema and in profile-edit from Phase 1, or Phase 3 search has nothing to filter on and the Recall story breaks. So: not in onboarding, but in the data model now.

## What I'm doing next

Writing the Phase 1 design spec - the flow, the exact copy, the light system, and what each screen does with the sky. That's the "MVP design version" you asked for, and it becomes the input to the design prompt you want to try.

Then look and feel split cleanly, which keeps us honest with the doc's rule that feel is settled in Xcode:

- **Look and copy** get settled in a visual mock you can hold on your phone. Color, density, spacing, wording.
- **Feel** gets settled on device in SwiftUI. Springs, gesture, haptics. A mock can't tell you anything true about those.

Starting the spec now. I'll show you the doc and we iterate from there rather than trying to land it in one shot.

# Phase 1 design: profile and onboarding

How a person goes from a fresh install to having a card.

`mvp-design.md` owns the architecture and the phase plan.
This file owns Phase 1's flow, copy, and the light system behind it.
`todo.md` tracks state.

## What Phase 1 delivers

A signed-in person can create their card, see it, and edit it.
That is the whole phase.

The card is the thing you hold up to someone.
Everything after Phase 1 (directory, search, connect) assumes it exists, so this is the floor the rest of the product stands on.

Phase 1 also carries the hero interaction: the card coming into being.
It is the moment we build to the full quality bar to learn what SwiftUI can actually do for us, and every screen after it inherits that standard.

## The design principle

Plain content, quiet light.
The magic is rare, and the user always causes it.

Haven has to feel like two things at once that normally fight each other.
It has to feel ordinary and safe, like a tool anyone belongs in.
It also has to feel quietly magical, like your presence in it matters.

The way those two live together is the way *Your Name* does it.
Most of that film is ordinary life: a classroom, a train, someone cooking dinner.
It is rendered with extraordinary attention to light, and the actually magical moments are rare and brief.
The film earns them by being quiet everywhere else.

So, concretely:

Layout, type, and copy stay plain.
Generous space, ordinary words, no ornament.
This is most of the app, and it is the part that says anyone belongs here.

Light is the only expressive material, and it lives behind content, never on top of it.
Nothing glows just to look nice.

Magic is rare and earned.
The card forming. A connection being made.
Not every tap.

Traces are caused, never decorative.
Light only moves in response to something the person did.
That is the difference between a memory and a screensaver.

### What this rules out

Bouncy startup-app motion, confetti, celebration states, badges, progress percentages, streaks.
Anything that glows on its own for decoration.
Copy that performs feeling instead of just being warm and clear.

## The light system

This is the spine of the phase, and it is not a metaphor bolted onto a form.
It runs on the sky we already built for the web app in `src/sky.ts`.

That file already does the hard part.
Every person gets a constellation minted deterministically from their name, so the same person has the same sky forever.
The figure is drawn with a minimum spanning tree, which is why it reads calm instead of criss-crossed.
Faint background dust is seeded from one fixed string so the whole sky twinkles as one, and it is kept deliberately dim so it never competes with a person's own stars.
The star data even carries a per-star `rvd` reveal seed, an ignition order, already built in.

Phase 1 spreads that ignition across the onboarding instead of playing it all at once.

### How it works

Before you enter a name, there is dust and nothing else.
You are not in the sky yet.

When you enter your name, your constellation is minted from it.
One star lights.

Every answer after that lights one more star, and an edge draws to connect it to the figure.

At the end, the figure completes and settles.
That is your card.

Fields you skipped are stars that have not lit yet.
They are visible, and they are dim.
That is the entire mechanism for getting optional fields filled in later: your sky is dimmer than it could be, and you can see it.
No badges, no completion bar, no nagging.

Your preferred contact method is the brightest star in the figure, and it is the one that earns a diffraction flare.
`sky.ts` already gives flares to the two brightest majors, so this is a matter of ordering, not new code.

### Rules this system has to obey

Each profile field maps to a fixed star index, decided once and never reshuffled.
If the mapping moved, your sky would rearrange every time you edited your profile, and the promise that your sky is permanently yours would be a lie.

Light responds to a committed value, not to keystrokes.
A star ignites when a field is saved, not while you are typing into it.

The sky never blocks input.
It is behind the content and it never delays a tap, a keyboard, or a continue button.

### The density reduction

The web sky is rich: 150 faint stars, three nebulae, five giants, seven or eight constellation stars, flares, and a shooting star.
Haven on iOS is minimalist, so the port is a reduction, not a copy.

Keep the system: deterministic per-person constellation, shared dim dust, stable identity.
Cut the density hard.

Exactly how far to cut is a look question, and it gets settled in the visual mock rather than argued about here.
The final constellation star count and the field-to-star slot list get fixed together, because the slots have to fit the figure.

## The flow

Seven steps, and every one of them is one question on one screen.

```
sign in -> opening -> name -> photo -> where -> socials -> preferred -> your card
             (mood)  (req)   (skip)   (skip)    (core)     (core)      (reveal)
```

The structure stays dead simple on purpose.
One question per screen, one big clear input, an obvious way forward, and an obvious way to skip anything optional.
The emotion lives in the presentation, not in the mechanics.
If someone has to work out what a screen is asking, the magic has cost more than it gave.

### 0. Sign in

Sign in with Apple first, then the other options.
Apple is required by App Store guideline 4.8 once any third-party login is offered, and it is the lowest-friction option anyway.

Custom SwiftUI screens calling Clerk underneath.
Phase 0 shipped with Clerk's prebuilt `AuthView`, which is a placeholder, and replacing it is Phase 1 work.

Sky: dust only, drifting slowly.

> Haven
>
> Keep the people you meet.

### 1. Opening

One screen that sets the mood and asks for nothing.

Sky: dust only. A few distant lights, no figure. The sky exists and you are not in it yet.

> You meet people all the time.
>
> Haven is where they stay.

Button: **Set up your card**

### 2. Name (required)

> What should people call you?

A single text field. The keyboard comes up on its own.
No helper text, no format rules, no character counter.

This is the only required field in the whole flow, because it is the one that mints your sky.

On commit: your constellation is minted from the name, and the first star lights.

### 3. Photo (optional)

> How should people recognize you?

Tap a circle to choose from your library or take one.

Skip: **Skip for now**

On set: the photo lands in the circle, a star lights, and an edge draws to it.

Needs a photo library permission string, and a camera one if we allow taking it here.

### 4. Where (optional)

> Where are you these days?

A plain city text field.
Not a map picker, not a location permission prompt.

Skip: **Skip for now**

Stored as a normalized lowercase string so Phase 3 can filter on it.
`convex/nameSearch.ts` already has `normalizeName` for exactly this kind of key.

On set: a star lights.

### 5. Socials (core)

> Where can people find you?

The one screen with more than one input, because these belong together.

Rows: Instagram, X, LinkedIn, Facebook, phone.
Tap a row to add a handle. Empty rows stay quiet and unstyled.
All of them are skippable, though skipping all of them makes for a card that cannot do much.

This is where most of the light in the flow comes from, which is correct, because this is the core of what a Haven card is for.

On each handle added: a star lights.

### 6. Preferred contact (core)

> Which one do you actually check?

A single choice, showing only the ones just filled in.

This gets its own screen rather than a checkmark next to a row on the previous one.
It is a different kind of question, a choice rather than an entry, and it is the single field the whole Reach loop pays off on.
Inline on a form screen, it would get skipped.

If exactly one social was filled in, it is preselected and the screen still shows, because confirming takes one tap and being wrong here breaks the point of the product.

On set: that star becomes the brightest in the figure and takes a flare.

### 7. Your card

The figure completes, the remaining edges draw, and it settles.
This is the hero moment of Phase 1.

> Your card is ready.

The card itself: name, photo, constellation, preferred contact.

A quiet line under it, stated once and never repeated as a nag:

> You can add more any time.

Button: **Done**

### After done

Done lands on the directory, which in Phase 1 is empty, because saving people is Phase 2.

That empty state needs real thought rather than a placeholder.
It is the first thing a new user sees after the best moment in the app, and a grey "No contacts yet" box would undo the whole flow.
The honest version of it is that the sky is yours and nobody else is in it yet.

## Editing later

Editing is not a re-run of the wizard.

My Card shows your card with every field, filled or empty.
Empty fields read as unlit, matching the sky.
Tapping any field edits that field alone.

Two fields live here that are deliberately not in onboarding: company and role.

They are cut from the flow because onboarding stays minimal, but they have to exist in the schema and in edit from Phase 1.
Phase 3 search filters on company, city, and role.
Without them there is nothing to filter on and the Recall story does not work.

Interests, hobbies, and conversation starters are cut from Phase 1 entirely, including from edit.
They were the right instinct to drop from onboarding, and adding them to edit now would be scope with no consumer.

## What this needs from the backend

The `profiles` table today is three fields: `userId`, `username`, `updatedAt`.
It was built for the old Haven Meet handle exchange.

Phase 1 needs it to hold name, photo, city, company, role, social handles, and preferred contact.

The change is additive.
New fields go on as optional, nothing existing changes shape.

That matters because the legacy web product is still live.
Signing in on the web still routes to the full old app (`resolveView` in `src/lib.ts:227`), and it still calls `profiles.getMyProfile`, `setUsername`, and `meetExchange`.
Reshaping the table to save a few nullable fields would break a working surface for no gain.

The photo needs Convex `_storage`, following the pattern `convex/captures.ts` already uses for screenshot uploads.

Convex functions keep the existing vitest TDD flow: write the failing test, implement, run the suite.

Separately, and not part of this phase: that legacy web product surface (`people`, `captures`, `loveAlarm`, `sharedNotes`) is now orphaned by the native pivot.
It should be either formally parked or deleted, as its own decision.

## Build order within Phase 1

The hero moment goes first, against a hardcoded profile.

It is pure motion, it needs no backend at all, and it is the only thing in this phase that can tell us the native bet was wrong.
Its whole stated purpose in `mvp-design.md` is to teach us our SwiftUI ceiling early rather than after four phases of plumbing.
Schema and CRUD are low-risk work that we might throw away if the ceiling disappoints, so they wait.

1. The card forming, hardcoded data, full quality bar
2. Extend the `profiles` schema and mutations, test-first
3. Onboarding and edit wired to real data, still behind the existing prebuilt auth screen
4. Photo upload
5. Replace the front door: custom sign-in UI with Sign in with Apple

Steps 3 and 5 split on purpose.
Building the profile half against the auth screen that already works means it is usable sooner, and the custom auth work blocks nothing.

## How look and feel get decided

They get decided in different places, and mixing them up wastes both.

Look and copy are settled in a visual mock, held on a phone.
Color, star density, spacing, type, wording.
A mock is good for these and it is fast to iterate.

Feel is settled on device in SwiftUI.
Springs, gesture, momentum, interruption, haptics.
A mock cannot tell you anything true about any of those, which is why `mvp-design.md` puts feel in Xcode previews rather than in a web prototype.

## Open questions

The density reduction, and with it the final constellation star count and the fixed field-to-star slot list.
Settled in the mock.

What the empty directory looks like after Done.

Whether the reveal is a transition from the last step or its own screen that you arrive at.
This is a feel question, so it gets answered on device.

`DESIGN.md` still carries the old Euno name and a web-oriented token set.
The iOS token set can start from it, but the rename pass is still outstanding across the repo.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Design plan before I build:

- **Color**: deep twilight ground (`#0B1020`), raised surface (`#131B33`), off-white ink with a lavender bias (`#E8E6F0`), indigo-biased grey (`#868CA6`), and one warm gold for lit stars (`#FFEBC7`). Gold is the only saturated thing on the page - everything else is quiet blue-grey. Light theme becomes pale dawn rather than an inversion.
- **Type**: warm system serif (`ui-serif`/Iowan Old Style) for the emotional copy, Apple system sans for UI text and labels. That split is honest - it's the same split the product has.
- **Layout**: a vertical sequence, phone on the left, explanation on the right, joined by a hairline that reads as a constellation edge. The page itself is the ignition sequence: scrolling down lights the constellation, one star per answered question.

The constellation is generated with the real algorithm from `sky.ts` - same FNV hash, same mulberry32, same Prim's spanning tree - so it's an actual Haven sky, not a drawing of one.

Haven · Phase 1

How someone gets a card

Seven steps from a fresh install to the thing you hold up to a person. One question per screen, and only the name is required. Every answer lights one star in a constellation that is yours permanently.

The principle

Plain content, quiet light. The magic is rare, and the user always causes it.

Most of Your Name is a classroom, a train, someone cooking dinner. It is ordinary life rendered with extraordinary attention to light, and the genuinely magical moments are rare and brief. The film earns them by being quiet everywhere else. Haven works the same way: plain layout, ordinary words, no ornament, and light as the only expressive material.

The light system

The onboarding is an ignition sequence

This is not a metaphor bolted onto a form. It runs on the deep-field sky already built and tested in src/sky.ts, where a person's constellation is minted from their name and stays theirs forever. The star data already carries a per-star reveal seed. Phase 1 spreads that ignition across the flow instead of playing it all at once.

Skipped fields are stars that have not lit yet. They stay visible and dim. That is the whole mechanism for getting optional fields filled in later, with no badges, no completion bar, and no nagging. Your sky is dimmer than it could be, and you can see it.

After Done

The empty directory matters

Done lands on the directory, which in Phase 1 is empty, because saving people is Phase 2. That empty state needs real thought rather than a placeholder. It is the first thing a person sees right after the best moment in the app, and a grey "No contacts yet" box would undo the whole flow. The honest version is that the sky is yours and nobody else is in it yet.

Decided

In the flow

  • Name is the only required field, because it mints the sky.
  • Photo and city are skippable in one tap.
  • Socials carry most of the light, because they are what a card is for.
  • Preferred contact gets its own screen, not a checkmark on a form row.

Deliberately not in the flow

  • Company and role are edit-only, but they ship in the schema now. Phase 3 search filters on company, city, and role, so without them Recall does not work.
  • Interests and hobbies are cut from Phase 1 entirely, including from edit. Adding them now would be scope with no consumer.

Still open

  • How far to cut the star density. The web sky has 150 faint stars; iOS is minimalist. Settled in a visual mock.
  • Whether the reveal is a transition or its own screen. A feel question, so it gets answered on device.
  • What the empty directory looks like.

Here's the flow, mapped out visually so you can judge it rather than read about it:

**https://claude.ai/code/artifact/45381fd6-1933-4757-9b27-dfb70236b861**

Scroll it. The page is the ignition sequence it describes - each step lights one more star as it comes into view. The constellation is generated with the actual algorithm from `src/sky.ts`, same hash, same seeded RNG, same spanning tree, so that's a real Haven sky, not a picture of one.

## The flow

```
sign in -> opening -> name -> photo -> where -> socials -> preferred -> your card
             (mood)  (req)   (skip)   (skip)    (core)     (core)      (reveal)
```

Eight screens. Five of them ask you something. Only your name is required, because it's the one that mints your sky.

The copy, in order: *What should people call you? / How should people recognize you? / Where are you these days? / Where can people find you? / Which one do you actually check?* Then: *Your card is ready.*

## The one idea worth arguing about

Your card starts as dust. No figure, you're not in the sky yet. Type your name and your constellation is minted from it, one star lights. Every answer after that lights one more and draws an edge to it. Your preferred contact ends up the brightest star and takes a flare.

**Skipped fields are stars that never lit.** They stay visible and dim. That's the whole mechanism for getting optional fields filled in later - no badges, no completion bar, no nagging. Your sky is dimmer than it could be and you can see it. On the final screen you'll spot two dim stars: company and role, waiting in edit.

## Decisions I made that you should push back on if you disagree

**Company and role stay in the schema even though they're cut from onboarding.** Phase 3 search filters on company, city, and role. Cut them entirely and Recall has nothing to filter on.

**Preferred contact gets its own screen** instead of a checkmark next to a row. It's the field the whole Reach loop pays off on, and inline on a form it gets skipped.

**Step 01 (Opening) is a screen with no input.** You said minimalist twice. This is the one screen that earns its place purely on feeling, and it's the most cuttable thing in the flow. Your call - the map makes it visible so you can decide.

## Also worth knowing

Phase 0 shipped with Clerk's prebuilt sign-in screen, so custom auth UI plus Sign in with Apple is still Phase 1 work. That's bigger than it sounds.

The `profiles` schema change stays additive, because signing in on the web still routes to the full old app and reads that table.

The risk now is the opposite of defensiveness: over-rotating into "lead with messaging" as a verdict, one day after the user pivoted to native, to prove you're not protecting the session's work. That's the mirror-image bias, and it's just as unjustified. Don't issue a directional verdict here. Issue the fork.

**The one thing that decides this is a value judgment only the user can make, and you've already found it:** their own docs carry two competing theses. "The phone is the product / feel is the product" vs. the Concerns section, where every deciding factor is friction and psychology. Those can't both be load-bearing. If feel is the product, messaging is *disqualified* — you get Apple's style guide, link previews instead of inline links, blue bubbles, zero control over the thing you said was everything. If friction is the enemy, messaging wins outright and attacks all three Concerns plus the re-engagement problem. So your reliable output isn't "lead with messaging" — it's "here's the fork, and which of your two theses is true decides it." Put that question back to them. That's the crux, and it's theirs.

**Weight the gate honestly — don't let the elegant "one product, two clients" framing bury it.** Your own research found: Poke is the *first* agent ever approved, it took months of compliance, it requires *live human customer-support availability*, and it's Business→Customer infrastructure that a personal-memory app fits only awkwardly. The Apple-approval risk is *never* in your hands. That's a strictly worse kind of dependency than the one they consciously accepted. Say that plainly.

**Fix one slip before you answer:** you're still floating WhatsApp as a test channel, but your own search said Meta barred general-purpose chatbots last fall. WhatsApp isn't available to Haven right now. The clean behavioral test is SMS via Twilio — and it's genuinely good: text a number, LLM parses, Convex stores, ask it recall questions. Keep that test. But scope it honestly to the user: it proves *the loop* (do I capture, do I come back to recall), not the delight, and not the channel. A janky grey-bubble SMS thread could produce a false null — don't let a weak result kill the idea, and don't let a strong one imply the Apple channel is solved.

**Also worth one line to the user:** Poke's traction doesn't transfer for free. Poke acts on your behalf (email, calendar) — texting a bot is natural for actions. Haven asks you to text intimate observations about *other people* into a bot thread and trust it as a store. That's a different, untested behavioral bet, which is exactly why the SMS test comes before the Apple paperwork.

The reassuring truth that lets them explore this without sunk-cost panic — lead with it: **the backend is invariant.** Convex, the three-table model, search, the auth seam — all of it serves both clients. Short answer: no, you don't strictly need a native app. Poke proved the channel is real - Apple approved them in June as the first AI agent on Messages for Business. So this isn't a hypothetical.

And the idea is better than it might look, because of something in your own doc.

## What messaging would actually buy you

Your Concerns section lists three unsolved problems and calls them "the things most likely to decide whether Haven actually works." A messaging interface attacks all three:

**Concern 1, friction to manually add people.** Right now that's a form. Over text it's one message: "met Sarah at Katrin, Amazon research team, wore a Spain shirt." No app switch, no fields, no breaking the conversation.

**Concern 2, friction to add dynamic context.** Your doc asks for "the lightest possible input, a sentence or a voice note, instead of structured fields." A message thread is literally that.

**Concern 3, swipe review assumes re-engagement that may not happen.** Messaging fixes this structurally. Haven can text *you*. That's the one channel people actually open.

There's a fourth thing. Your search contract admits MVP search can't handle natural language and warns that users must never be invited to type a sentence that returns nothing. Over messaging, a sentence is the only interface, and an LLM makes it work. Recall gets *better*, not worse.

## What it costs you

**The feel thesis.** On Messages for Business you get Apple's style guide, link previews instead of inline links, and blue bubbles. Zero control. Everything we designed today - the ignition, the constellation, the card forming - is gone from the interaction. You said feel is the product. Messaging is the one architecture where you have none of it.

**A gate you don't control.** This is the part I'd weigh hardest. Poke is the *first* agent ever approved.
